precepts.text: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary! So we are the widow. Christ is making reference back to that in Luke 18.
precepts.point: Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? Will there be faith? Will brothers and sisters still be doing that? That is the question. Will you believe to pray for vengeance? Will you believe that thing? That is what Christ is asking.

note.label: The Waters of Noah Will Be Fire

precepts.why:
In the parable “there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary.” We are that widow. The Lord said he was married unto us, but because we sinned, he refused us. Jeremiah shows the same widow: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow!”

“she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary”! That is Israel: once full of people, great among the nations, a princess among the provinces, now alone, cast off like a widow, and paying tribute to others. Christ is making reference back to that in Luke 18.

So the widow crying “Avenge me of mine adversary” is us, the twelve tribes, crying for vengeance on our enemies. We want revenge. “he would not for a while”, just as the Lord kept silence for a time, but “because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.” Because the twelve tribes trouble him, he will avenge her. That is the key: pray for vengeance and don't stop.

“And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him”? We are the elect, crying day and night, three times a day. Some of our people call it unjust that God put us in slavery and punished us, and ask why an all-loving God would do that. It is not unjust: you punish your kids when they go off, and likewise the Lord. “I tell you that he will avenge them speedily.” The question Christ asks is whether, when he comes, he will find that faith: will the widow still be praying for vengeance?

precepts.text: The parable for those who trust in themselves that they are righteous and despise others: the sinner who humbled himself went down justified.
precepts.point: The publican went home justified rather than the other. Everyone that exalts himself shall be abased, as Manasseh was locked up, and he that humbles himself shall be exalted, as Manasseh was later; and you will not like the humbling.

note.label: The Mercy and Humility of King Manasseh

precepts.why:
Manasseh prays, “I am not worthy to behold and see the height of heaven for the multitude of mine iniquities.” Many of us think this. Christ gives a parable about that very man, spoken “unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others.” Those who were righteous in their own eyes and despised everybody else were the Pharisees: I'm more righteous than you, you're wicked.

“Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.” The publican was a tax collector, and they were praying in the same place. The Pharisee thanked God he was “not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican”, not like this dude next to him, and bragged, “I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.”

“And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven.” Why? Because he felt unworthy, the same as Manasseh, who could not behold the height of heaven. He “smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner”: the same thing Manasseh said in his prayer, my sins are a multitude.

Christ's judgment: “this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.” The sinner who asked for mercy went home justified; the one who called himself righteous did not. “for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased”: that is what Manasseh did in the beginning, exalting himself, and he was brought down to a low condition, locked up and imprisoned. “and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted”: that is Manasseh later on, after he humbled himself.

So humble yourself and you will be exalted. Exalt yourself and you will be humbled, and you are not going to like that humbling either.

precepts.text: The unjust judge avenged the widow for her continual coming; how much more shall God avenge His own elect speedily, yet shall He find faith on earth when the Son of man cometh.
precepts.point: We ask the question, how long shall the wicked triumph.

note.label: Psalm 94: The God of Vengeance and Defense of His People

precepts.why:
“O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself.” We really have to understand this in these times when a lot of our brothers and sisters want to take up arms against the oppressor, because vengeance belongeth to the Most High. Christ gave the parable: “There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him, saying, Avenge me of mine adversary. And he would not for a while: but afterward he said within himself, Though I fear not God, nor regard man; Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.”

The unjust judge avenged the widow for her continual coming. “And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? I tell you that he will avenge them speedily.” How much more shall God avenge his own elect who cry day and night unto him, even though he bear long with them.

That is the answer to “how long shall the wicked triumph?” We keep crying to him like the widow, and he will avenge speedily. But Christ ends with the warning: “Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?” Shall he find faith on earth when the Son of man comes, or will we have taken up arms and stopped waiting on him?

precepts.point: They compassed me about also with words of hatred and fought against me without a cause. For my love they are my adversaries, but I give myself unto prayer. We have to give ourselves unto prayer and let God fight our battles, for it is not by our might.
precepts.why:
“For my love they are my adversaries: but I give myself unto prayer.” Luke 18 is where Christ shows what giving yourself unto prayer looks like.

When the nations compass us about with words of hatred and fight against us without a cause, we have to give ourselves unto prayer and let God fight our battles, for it is not by our might.

The souls of the righteous ask God, when are you going to avenge us? Christ said the same thing. Remember, that is in heaven; Christ gave a parable and taught us to pray for vengeance. Christians are going to get mad at this part, because you have never been taught this in your church; it is blasphemous to talk about this. “And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;” The subject matter is prayer, and don't give up praying. “Saying, There was in a city a judge, which feared not God, neither regarded man: And there was a widow in that city; and she came unto him,” This widow represents the Israelites; the unjust judge represents God. “saying, Avenge me of mine adversary.” This widow woman with no husband goes to the unjust judge and says, I need you to avenge me of my adversary. “And he would not for a while:” The unjust judge didn't listen to the widow; he didn't want to hear nothing she had to say; he ignored her. “but afterward he said within himself,” Time has passed. “Though I fear not God,” There is no one above me, I don't believe in it. “nor regard man;” I don't regard man on earth. “Yet because this widow troubleth me,” This woman whose husband died keeps bothering me, asking for vengeance, annoying me in her prayers. “I will avenge her,” I will avenge her. “lest by her continual coming she weary me.”

Here is the point, and here is the breakdown, so you know it is the right breakdown. “And the Lord said, Hear what the unjust judge saith.” Christ said to us, now hear what the unjust judge said. “And shall not God avenge his own elect,” Shall not the Father avenge the Israelites, “which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them?” Though he bear long with the Israelites. “I tell you that he will avenge them speedily.” He will avenge them speedily. “Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?” You know why he asked that? Because some of you don't believe that; you think it is evil to pray for vengeance. Will there be faith on the earth? Why? Because we have white supremacy in our mind; we think it is evil to pray for vengeance. It is not talking about praying for vengeance against your brother; it is talking about the other nations, of course.

You ever notice when a cop kills a black kid and our people are rioting in the streets, every time the parent comes out they say stuff like let's all be at peace, let's just love each other? We are quick to forgive. Mike Brown's mother went out and said burn this down; the Jackal said come with me in the back, not only will we charge you and your husband for all the destruction out here, you are going to spend the rest of your time in jail; she had to go back and recant her statement. We are not allowed to say it, although in your mind you want everything destroyed, because your kid has just been murdered. So Christ gave us the solution. Look at that church in Charleston, South Carolina, where all the black people got put to death by that Edomite: think of the mentality, they say we forgive him. That is a slave mentality. All your friends and relatives have just been murdered, the cops take the dude to Burger King, and you are sitting there saying we forgive him in the name of Jesus. What Bible are you reading? You are listening to Cesare. South Carolina in particular is a slave port with all kinds of slavery history, and those brothers and sisters in that church had their mind on channel zero; they have not been learning the Bible at all.

Christ told us to pray for vengeance. At night we are supposed to ask the Lord for vengeance against our enemies, those that destroyed our ancestors. That is a righteous thing with God, and that is for the living. When we are dead we are going to say it again: Lord, wait, are you going to avenge us? And the Lord says, not yet, just wait. We saw it with Botham Jean's family: a mockery, a slap in the face of ignorant black people, the court-appointed judge rubbing the white woman's hair and giving her her personal Bible, the brother coming up and giving her a hug, and the white man sitting back saying great job, their system is working like clockwork, we don't have to do nothing more, we have these idiots right where we want them, lost and destroyed. Now she has filed an appeal to have her sentence shortened, rather than serve her ten, and in the lawsuit the family is not getting any money: since you all loved her so much, your brother obviously wouldn't want her hurt financially. Black people are worse than cockroaches sometimes. They get mad when we say black people, but the Most High is making a separation between the Israelites and black people. You black people, there is no hope for you; your hope is in Obama, voting, getting money, and the scriptures show there are principalities and dark forces in high places that can only be taken down by God. There is no man on earth that can right the wrongs we face every single day, but they want you in the church praying and singing and voting and hoping and idolizing basketball players instead of waiting for your Savior to come. They have you right where they want you.

“And shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him”: that’s what our people are doing on earth, and in the spirit realm those that have died are doing the same thing. Christ commanded us to pray for vengeance against our enemies.
